one_line_idea: Claimed viewpoint invariance of self-supervised ViT features collapses at a measurable camera-baseline knee, and the knee position, not average similarity, predicts a backbone's 3D utility.

Geometric information in vision foundation models peaks in middle transformer blocks, so standard last-layer feature extraction systematically understates and misranks the 3D awareness of 2D backbones.

Learned feature upsamplers make features look sharper while corrupting the sub-pixel geometric signal, so pipelines that match or triangulate upsampled features get worse 3D estimates than bilinear baselines.

Image-text contrastive features are not geometry-poor: controlling for resolution and probe capacity, their coarse depth-ordering knowledge matches self-supervised features, and the reported gap is a protocol artifact.
Foundation features carry a systematic metric-scale bias inherited from the crop-scale distribution of pretraining augmentations, measurable as a predictable error in apparent-size judgments.

Under controlled synthetic viewpoint sweeps, generative-diffusion features are not more multi-view consistent than contrastive features once texture density is controlled, contradicting a growing assumption in 3D distillation work.
A measurable fraction of reported 3D awareness in ViT probes is absolute positional-embedding leakage: probes read where a patch is in the frame, not what geometry the features encode.
Textureless-surface correspondence failure of foundation features is a token-granularity artifact, and dense overlapping-stride re-extraction recovers most of it without any retraining.

Decomposing 2D features into view-invariant and view-dependent components before lifting them into 3D feature fields yields more geometrically faithful fields than the standard practice of averaging raw features across views.

Jointly distilling 2D semantic features into Gaussian-splat scenes measurably degrades the recovered geometry relative to photometric-only optimization, a cost the feature-field literature does not report.

Foundation features cannot disambiguate the front and back of near-symmetric objects, and the error direction is predicted by canonical-pose frequency in web imagery, making pose pipelines built on them systematically biased rather than randomly wrong.

The believed semantics-versus-geometry fine-tuning tradeoff in foundation backbones is a protocol artifact: tuning only late blocks at small learning rates buys large geometry gains at near-zero semantic cost.
Monocular depth foundation models infer focal length implicitly from image content, and their metric-depth errors are largely explained by the error of that hidden focal estimate.

Generalization of monocular depth models scales with scene-layout diversity of training data, not raw image count, and layout-diversity-matched subsets can replicate full-data performance at a fraction of the size.

Teacher-student pseudo-label distillation, the engine of current depth foundation models, systematically erodes depth discontinuities with each generation, measurable as monotonic depth-edge degradation across distillation rounds.
Ordinal errors of relative-depth models concentrate at object-ground contact ambiguities, so a contact-focused probe set exposes large headroom that whole-image ranking metrics hide.

Detected object instances of known physical size classes act as an implicit calibration rig: a post-hoc scale solver over class-size priors converts relative depth to metric depth competitively with intrinsics-aware models on populated scenes.
Depth foundation models fail on non-pinhole imagery with a characteristic radial error signature, and a lens-conditioned resampling wrapper recovers most of the loss without retraining the backbone.
Restricting test-time adaptation of video depth to per-sequence scale-shift-bias parameters under multi-view photometric consistency gives robust cross-domain gains where full-model TTA collapses.

A linear readout on frozen self-supervised features already sits within a small margin of specialized depth architectures on standard benchmarks, implying the benchmarks no longer measure depth-decoder research.

Low-light depth degradation of foundation models is dominated by a structured, exposure-predictable bias rather than variance, so a tiny exposure-conditioned correction head recovers most of the loss without retraining.

Small-baseline temporal parallax in casual video contains enough signal to resolve metric scale without IMU or intrinsics, and current video depth models fail to exploit it, as revealed by a parallax-ablation test.

Ad hoc sky handling in depth training pipelines systematically distorts far-field geometry and horizon placement, and the distortion is measurable and correctable with a principled at-infinity parameterization.
Depth foundation models are substantially worse in the near-field manipulation zone (under 1 meter) than benchmark averages imply, because standard benchmarks under-sample exactly that range.

Optical flow benchmarks hide an unsolved motion-blur regime: blur-stratified evaluation will show error concentrating on high-blur pixels, where current models degrade to near-uselessness while averages look solved.

Iterative recurrent refinement in flow architectures is largely an inference-time crutch: a single-pass global-matching model with a strong upsampler can match refinement-based accuracy at a fraction of latency on high-resolution video.

Flow models track texture translation, not motion: on isoluminant color motion and other texture-decoupled stimuli they will fail catastrophically, exposing that learned flow lacks the motion-energy computation biological vision has.

On mostly-static scenes, point-tracking benchmark performance is largely explained by camera-geometry propagation, so learned trackers should be credited only for their margin over a depth-plus-pose geometric baseline.
Long-horizon point-tracking failures are dominated by re-identification errors after occlusion, not accumulated drift, so drift-focused architectural work targets the wrong failure mode.
Epipolar-constrained self-supervision on unlabeled real video can close most of the synthetic-to-real gap in optical flow, ending the field's structural dependence on synthetic training data.

Scalar end-point error hides direction errors that dominate downstream time-to-contact and steering computations, and a direction-magnitude decomposed evaluation reorders the flow leaderboard for safety-relevant use.

Explicit multi-hypothesis track states with a lightweight reappearance detector can match heavyweight learned-memory trackers on occlusion recovery at a fraction of compute, showing occlusion handling is a state-representation problem, not a capacity problem.
Monocular feed-forward 4D reconstruction now implies scene flow good enough to rival LiDAR-supervised methods for medium-range dynamics, collapsing a sensor requirement into a software capability.

Flow models carry a resolution-specific motion prior: evaluated off their training resolution they systematically underestimate large motions in a way predictable from correlation-volume truncation, not random degradation.

Point trackers trained on rigid-dominated data fail on non-rigid shear and stretching in a structured way: they snap to texture landmarks and refuse continuous deformation, measurable on procedurally deformed surfaces.

Temporal context beyond two frames pays for itself almost entirely inside occluded regions: multi-frame flow gains are an occlusion-inpainting effect, and reporting occluded/visible strata separately will prove it and redirect multi-frame architecture design.

Densify-and-split in Gaussian splatting is an implicit coarse-to-fine annealing schedule, and its scheduling, not the adaptive heuristics, carries most of the quality, testable by matched-budget schedule ablations.

Spherical-harmonic color in Gaussian splatting mostly compensates residual geometric error rather than modeling reflectance: fixing geometry with ground truth collapses the benefit of higher SH orders.

Beyond a scene-dependent primitive budget, additional Gaussians fit view-sampling noise: interpolated-view metrics keep improving while extrapolated-view quality degrades, an overfitting signature current protocols never measure.

With opacity-entropy and surface-concentration regularization, splat scenes can serve as measurement-grade geometry, closing most of the surface-accuracy gap to multi-view-stereo pipelines while keeping real-time rendering.
Anti-aliasing filters in splatting can be replaced by letting each primitive learn its own scale-space response, removing hand-derived filter approximations and their failure cases at extreme zoom.

Splatting failures on mirror-like surfaces are optimization pathologies, not representational limits: with reflection-consistent initialization the standard representation converges to virtual-image geometry that renders correctly from held-out views.

Feed-forward splat predictors fail on camera-baseline distribution shift, not scene-content shift: their generalization boundary is a property of the training rig geometry, measurable by a baseline-sweep protocol.

Floater artifacts in splat reconstructions are primarily fossilized exposure and white-balance inconsistency, not sparse-view ambiguity: photometric-nuisance-controlled captures will eliminate most floaters at unchanged view counts.

Splat compression methods pass interpolation benchmarks while selectively destroying view-extrapolation ability, so compression papers systematically overstate fidelity for any consumer that leaves the capture path.

Dynamic splat representations interpolate time but cannot extrapolate it even fractions of a second, revealing they store appearance trajectories rather than motion models, measurable by a future-rendering cliff test.

Popping artifacts in splat rendering are localized depth-ordering errors fixable by exact small-k per-tile sorting only where a cheap ambiguity test triggers, giving artifact-free video at a bounded few-percent cost.

Implicit neural fields still beat explicit splats decisively on thin structures and view extrapolation, and a structure-stratified benchmark will show the representations are complements, not a settled succession.

Feed-forward pointmap reconstructors carry strong absolute scene-scale priors and will misreconstruct scale-anomalous scenes (miniatures, sets, macro shots) in a predictable direction, revealing memorized scale rather than inferred geometry.

Pose-free reconstruction models contain an implicit camera-intrinsics estimator whose bias is set by the training field-of-view distribution, and their pose errors on out-of-distribution lenses are predictable from that bias alone.

Multi-task 3D foundation models suffer measurable gradient conflict between depth and pose heads specifically on dynamic-scene batches, and conflict-gated task weighting recovers accuracy on both without new data.

Neural surface reconstruction can reach near-GT-supervised accuracy using only photometric and multi-view consistency, and a controlled supervision-ablation study will locate exactly which scenes still need 3D ground truth.

Scaling feed-forward 3D reconstruction is data-limited, not parameter-limited: multi-view scene data has low effective diversity per token, and a compute-matched scaling study will show exponents far below those driving 2D and language scaling optimism.

Recurrent-memory reconstruction models have an effective spatial memory horizon of only a few keyframes: a loop-revisitation probe will show geometry consistency decaying with intervening content, exposing sequential state as the bottleneck for long-form 3D perception.

Full cross-view attention in reconstruction transformers is mostly spent rediscovering epipolar geometry: constraining attention to epipolar neighborhoods after a coarse pose estimate retains accuracy at large compute savings.

Single-image 3D generators are dominated by canonical-shape retrieval: counterfactual probes that decouple texture identity from geometric evidence will show outputs following the recognized category, not the visible geometry.

Rolling-shutter skew and motion blur are exploitable metric side channels: they encode absolute velocity and hence absolute scale, recoverable by a learned estimator to metrically calibrate monocular reconstruction without IMU or intrinsics.

Elaborate positional encodings in point cloud transformers are mostly redundant with kNN graph topology: an encoding-ablation study will show local connectivity carries the signal, collapsing a crowded design axis.

Object-centric 3D pretraining transfers poorly to scene-level tasks because it learns closed-surface completion priors that actively mislead on open scene geometry, a measurable negative-transfer effect.

Masked point-cloud pretraining learns sensor sampling patterns more than geometry: cross-sensor transfer tests will show performance collapse that tracks sampling-density mismatch rather than shape content.

Built-in rotation invariance in point cloud architectures destroys pose information that registration and manipulation actually need, and augmentation-trained equivariant-by-learning models dominate on a pose-sensitivity-stratified task suite.

Lifting frozen 2D foundation features onto 3D points already saturates much of what 3D self-supervised learning achieves, so 3D SSL should be measured by its margin over the 2D-lifting baseline, which is rarely reported.

Learned registration features fail in the low-overlap regime for a specific reason, local ambiguity without global layout reasoning, and overlap-stratified evaluation plus a layout-hypothesis stage will both prove and fix it.

Point cloud upsampling networks hallucinate plausible-looking surface detail that measurably corrupts downstream pose estimation and registration, making upsampling a negative-value preprocessing step for geometric pipelines.

Discarding range-image structure by converting scans to unordered points throws away the sensor noise model, and architectures that retain scan-grid structure will beat point-set models on odometry at matched capacity.

Content-adaptive keyframe selection, not longer context, is the binding constraint in long-video understanding: a learned selector at 10% frame budget can retain nearly all of full-context accuracy across video reasoning tasks.

For revisitation-heavy long videos, a geometric 3D scene buffer beats learned appearance-token memories of the SAM2 style at re-localizing content after long absences, because place is a stronger long-horizon key than appearance.

Video self-supervised representations pass action benchmarks largely on static appearance: dynamics-isolating probes (motion-only stimuli, frame-shuffle controls) will show most benchmark skill survives temporal destruction.

Long-video benchmarks are answerable from tiny frame subsets: an oracle frame-selection audit will show most questions need under 1% of frames, meaning the benchmarks measure retrieval, not long-form temporal understanding.
Video foundation models are near chance at judging the arrow of time on physics-driven footage, a capability gap invisible to every mainstream benchmark and decisive for world-model claims.

Event-order understanding in video-language models rides on editing artifacts: on continuous single-shot footage their before/after accuracy will collapse, revealing shot grammar, not temporal reasoning, as the learned mechanism.

Storing motion state (tracked positions, velocities, and a sparse dynamics summary) instead of appearance tokens halves video-memory cost at equal long-horizon tracking accuracy, because appearance is re-observable but motion history is not.

Video models encode absolute frame rate as a hidden covariate: speed-perception probes will reveal systematic bias when test frame rate differs from the training distribution, corrupting all downstream motion judgments.
Repetitive-action counting is already latent in frozen video features as periodic token-trajectory structure, extractable by spectral analysis without any counting-specific training.

The egocentric-video performance gap is mostly a camera-motion-statistics gap, not a content gap: motion-matched resampling of exocentric data will close much of it without collecting new egocentric footage.

Video models covertly exploit codec structure: evaluated on artifact-free renders or re-encoded footage, motion-sensitive task performance will shift measurably, revealing compression as an unacknowledged input feature.

Pixel-space next-frame prediction spends its capacity on texture advection, not dynamics: a loss-decomposition study will show physics-relevant errors are a vanishing share of the training signal, explaining why video predictors fail physics probes despite low loss.

Object permanence in video trackers and memory models fails past a measurable occlusion-duration threshold, and the failure is architectural (memory decay) rather than perceptual, testable by a duration-sweep protocol with location prediction through occlusion.

Lifting multi-object tracking into reconstructed 3D turns heavy occlusion from a failure regime into a solvable geometry problem: 3D-buffer tracking will dominate 2D association precisely in the occlusion-density stratum where benchmarks are hardest.

Feed-forward dynamic-scene reconstruction can match per-scene-optimized 4D methods on geometry metrics within a bounded gap while being orders faster, making optimization-based 4D a transitional technology, and the gap map tells us where optimization still pays.

Piecewise-rigid motion priors generalize to fast, unfamiliar dynamics better than learned free-form deformation fields, and a motion-magnitude-stratified 3D tracking comparison will show the crossover point where learned flexibility becomes a liability.

Video-diffusion priors in dynamic reconstruction pipelines improve photorealism metrics while leaving geometric accuracy unchanged or worse, and a geometry-photometrics decomposed evaluation will expose the conflation driving their adoption.

Discrete keyframe-based 4D representations with learned interpolators beat continuously time-conditioned fields on rapidly changing scenes, because continuous conditioning imposes an implicit temporal smoothness prior that fast dynamics violate.

Camera-object motion separation in monocular dynamic reconstruction degenerates predictably under near-forward camera motion, and quantifying the degeneracy prevalence in real corpora will show it affects a large share of driving and walking footage.

Transporting a fixed set of Gaussians along estimated scene flow, instead of re-densifying per timestep, reconstructs dynamic scenes with severalfold fewer primitives at equal quality, because dynamic scenes reuse geometry that current 4D methods keep re-creating.

Temporal smoothing losses that make video depth look stable actively destroy true depth change, and an approach-sequence evaluation (time-to-contact fidelity) will show stabilized models are worse than their unstabilized versions for dynamic consumers.

Classical low-rank trajectory bases still beat learned motion representations for non-rigid structure recovery on low-texture deformable objects, defining a data-regime boundary the deep 4D literature ignores.
Rolling-shutter row-time diversity within single frames can be exploited to super-resolve scene motion in time, recovering intra-frame 3D dynamics that global-shutter pipelines timestamp away.

Dynamic novel-view benchmarks are dominated by photometric quality variance rather than geometric fidelity: re-scoring published-style comparisons with geometry-only metrics will reorder methods and change which research directions look promising.

Defocus gradients across the frame are a single-image focal-length oracle: a probe exploiting depth-of-field structure will estimate intrinsics better than semantic-cue baselines, upgrading uncalibrated 3D pipelines for free.

Visual gravity-direction estimation from object and scene priors can reach IMU-competitive accuracy on typical footage, enabling orientation-aware vision on the billions of cameras without inertial data streams.

Out-of-distribution failure in learned camera pose regression is substantially a rotation-parameterization artifact: controlled parameterization swaps will show geodesic-aware outputs generalizing far better than the field's default choices at identical backbones.

Uncorrected radial distortion in training data leaves depth foundation models with a systematic depth-bowing fingerprint, detectable on flat surfaces and attributable to lens-distribution bias of the training corpora.

A camera-height prior over human-captured video (eye level and chest level dominate) yields metric scale within useful bounds for most consumer footage, formalizable as a drop-in probabilistic scale module for monocular pipelines.

Learned feature matchers win correspondence recall but lose sub-pixel precision to classical refinement: a hybrid that re-refines learned matches with classical photometric optimization will cut bundle-adjustment residuals without losing robustness.

Non-overlapping multi-camera rigs can be extrinsically calibrated to sub-degree accuracy using only a shared ground plane and per-camera odometry, removing the overlap requirement that constrains rig design.

The self-supervised depth-flow-pose triad is not saturated: joint reliability weighting across the three estimators (each downweighting pixels where the others disagree) yields large gains in adverse conditions where each alone degrades unpredictably.

Novel-view-synthesis metric families disagree enough to flip method rankings at publication-relevant margins, and a metric-agreement audit across the published method spectrum will quantify how much NVS progress is metric-choice artifact.

Chamfer distance is blind to topological errors that decide downstream success: a topology-aware reconstruction metric validated against robot navigation and interaction outcomes will re-rank reconstruction methods by fitness for use.

Point-tracking benchmark averages hide that leading models are still poor on thin structures and self-similar textures: difficulty-stratified re-annotation of existing benchmarks will reveal large headroom the leaderboard says does not exist.

The claimed closure of the synthetic-to-real gap in optical flow does not survive rolling-shutter and exposure realities: real-camera-artifact-stratified evaluation will reopen the gap that clean benchmark transfers declared closed.

A meaningful share of recent indoor-reconstruction leaderboard movement is attributable to mesh post-processing choices rather than model improvements, and a standardized-backend re-evaluation will separate the two contributions method by method.

Label-free evaluation of video and 3D perception via internal geometric consistency (reconstruction closure across views and time) correlates strongly with supervised rankings, enabling benchmark-free model selection on any target domain.

LLM tool routing in vision-agent frameworks follows tool-description semantics rather than measured tool competence: swapping two overlapping tools' natural-language descriptions redirects most calls while implementations stay fixed.

A tiny logistic router over cheap image/query features matches frontier-LLM tool-choice quality in vision-agent pipelines, indicating that current orchestration 'reasoning' contributes little beyond surface features.

Vision-agent controllers cannot consume numeric tool metadata: decisive detector scores or OCR quality values injected into tool outputs change downstream decisions in only a small fraction of cases where they should flip the decision.
When-to-call-a-tool decisions improve more from a two-line self-probe ('answer without the tool, then estimate what the tool would add') than from scaling the controller model.

Vision-agent answers depend on tool call order even when evidence is commutative: permuting the order of independent tool calls flips final answers at a rate comparable to swapping the controller model itself.

Routing policies can improve without human labels by fine-tuning the controller on its own execution traces filtered by end-task self-consistency, because traces contain enough outcome signal to supervise tool choice.

System accuracy versus toolbox size is non-monotone: pruning a vision-agent's toolbox with a held-out marginal-utility score beats the full toolbox, because overlapping tools create routing confusion that outweighs coverage gains.

LLM controllers are near-chance at detecting silently corrupted tool outputs, but a cheap paired-call wrapper (re-run the tool on a jittered input and compare) restores most detection without touching the controller.
Auto-generated 'competence cards' — per-tool accuracy profiles measured on a small probe suite and inserted into the controller prompt — improve routing more than hand-written tool descriptions.

Orchestration prompts and routing policies tuned on one controller LLM transfer poorly to another: the cross-controller transfer penalty exceeds the tuning gain itself, making agent-framework results controller-specific claims.

Agent loops that pass localization results as numeric coordinates lose to loops that render the same results as visual marks on the image: the interface encoding, not the information content, drives the gap.

Prose tool reports cause downstream attribute hallucination: a traceable share of final-answer errors originates at the verbalization step rather than in the vision tool or the controller's reasoning, and structured key-value reports cut this error class.
Information loss across chained text handoffs compounds superlinearly: two verbalization steps lose more than twice one step's information, because each step re-summarizes an already-lossy summary.

Replacing the text handoff between a vision tool and the controller with a small learned adapter that injects continuous tokens recovers most of the interface-lost accuracy, isolating discretization — not controller reasoning — as the binding constraint.

Making tool reports question-aware — forwarding the user question to the tool's report generator — beats upgrading to a larger controller, because relevance filtering at the interface dominates reasoning capacity downstream.

Referring-expression drift is a loop failure, not a VLM failure: multi-turn agents lose object identity as similar-object count grows, and assigning persistent visual IDs (numbered marks) at first sight eliminates most identity errors without changing any model.

Agent pipelines exhibit round-number bias in quantitative visual estimates that single-pass VLMs do not: repeated verbalization quantizes sizes, counts, and distances toward salient round values, and the bias grows with loop depth.

For multi-step visual tasks, storing history as image crops beats storing text summaries at matched context budget: text memory, not context length, is the binding constraint on long-horizon visual agents.

A task-agnostic 'interface bandwidth' score — measured by freezing tools and controller and swapping only the interface encoding — predicts which task families an agent framework will fail on before any end-to-end evaluation.

Self-consistency voting saturates almost immediately for perception-bound questions because samples share the same wrong percept: the accuracy-vs-samples curve flattens by k=4 while reasoning-bound questions keep climbing.

Longer reasoning chains between looking and answering degrade fine-grained visual accuracy: forced chain length causally increases detail errors, indicating that verbal reasoning overwrites visual detail in the loop's working state.

For perception-bound tasks, spending test-time compute on re-looking (fresh encodes of question-relevant crops) dominates spending it on re-thinking (more reasoning tokens) at every matched budget point.

Best-of-N with a same-model verifier fails for perception because proposer and verifier share percepts: verification gains track proposer-verifier error decorrelation, and cross-encoder verifiers recover most of the oracle gap.

An allocation policy that spends crops and samples per-instance based on a cheap difficulty probe beats uniform allocation at fixed total budget, because the marginal utility of test-time compute varies by an order of magnitude across instances.

Iterative zooming is an anytime algorithm with a predictable profile: the first zoom captures most of the achievable gain on natural-image tasks, and only small-object long-tail tasks keep gaining past two steps.

A task decomposability score predicts when deep agent loops with a small VLM beat a large VLM at matched FLOPs: loops win only above a decomposability threshold, and the crossover is stable across task families.
Voting over agent-chosen image transformations beats voting over random augmentations at equal vote count: choosing which views to aggregate is itself a perceptual skill the loop can exploit.

Most of a perception loop's gain can be distilled into a single forward pass by fine-tuning on the loop's own successful traces, implying the loop is primarily a data generator rather than an inference-time necessity.

Perception tasks split into compute-limited and representation-limited families with a measurable signature: cross-sample answer variance under test-time compute predicts whether any loop can help, before running any loop.

Self-correction in vision agents fixes reasoning slips but not perception errors: revision rates conditioned on error type are strongly asymmetric because the loop re-reads its own percept instead of re-perceiving.

Below a measurable critic-precision threshold, verify-then-revise loops are net negative: flips from correct to wrong outnumber repairs, and the break-even precision can be estimated in advance from the flip matrix.
Requiring critics to cite pixel evidence — a crop or mark accompanying every objection — turns marginal verification loops into positive ones, because ungrounded objections drive most wrong flips.

Structured visual outputs should be verified visually: rendering predicted boxes or layouts back onto the image and asking a fresh model 'is this consistent' catches error classes that text-based verification of the same predictions never flags.

Self-verification loops have attractors: iterating verify-revise converges within a few steps to answers that are stable but wrong on a measurable fraction of instances, and convergence speed does not predict correctness.

Verifying visual claims via entailed consequence questions ('if X, then Y should be visible — check Y') outperforms direct re-asking, because consequence checks decorrelate the verifier's percept from the proposer's.
Revision gains decay geometrically across rounds with a stable ratio: one revision captures most of the achievable repair, making multi-round self-correction schedules mostly wasted compute.

A small library of specialized critics keyed to a fixed visual-error taxonomy (mislocalization, miscount, attribute swap, relation flip, hallucinated object) beats one general critic at equal cost, because critic instructions act as error priors.

Verifiers inherit proposer percepts through the transcript: verifiers shown only the image and the bare answer catch more perception errors than verifiers shown the full chain-of-thought, reversing the assumed value of context.
Step-level verification of intermediate tool outputs beats final-answer verification for multi-step visual tasks at matched verification budget, and the advantage grows with chain length.

Visual programs beat end-to-end VLM answering only above a measurable compositional-depth threshold: below it the program machinery is pure overhead, and the crossover depth is stable across program frameworks.

Most visual-program failures collapse into a short list of primitive-misuse patterns, so a fixed library of about ten automatic repair rules recovers a large share of failed executions without improving the planner.

Program abstractions assume deterministic subroutines, but resampling stochastic primitives flips visual-program answers at a rate that rivals planner-quality differences, making single-run program evaluations unstable as system claims.

Visual programs are less faithful than they look: when a primitive fails silently, controllers often emit answers from language priors while presenting them as program outputs, and counterfactual step-perturbation quantifies how often execution is bypassed.

Real query streams concentrate on few program skeletons, so caching and re-instantiating the top skeletons amortizes synthesis: coverage-vs-cache-size follows a heavy-tailed law exploitable for systems.

Adding a lightweight type system over visual-program primitives (region, entity-set, scalar, boolean) prevents a major share of wrong answers, because type confusion at step boundaries — not planning — is the dominant failure.

Planners told each primitive's empirical error profile write different and better programs — inserting redundancy and cross-checks where primitives are weak — showing program synthesis should condition on tool reliability, not just tool signatures.

Disagreement among multiple valid programs synthesized for the same query detects question ambiguity, not model failure: program-set disagreement predicts human answer disagreement and triggers useful clarification requests.

Visual programs are their own data engines: executing synthesized programs on procedurally generated scenes yields verified supervision that fine-tunes the planner, improving synthesis on real queries without human labels.

Visual programs make failures locally attributable in a way chain-of-thought does not: automatic step-level attribution on synthetic scenes assigns blame to the true faulty step far above chance, enabling targeted fixes impossible for monolithic VLMs.

Annotation agents make correlated errors across seeds and prompt variants, so self-agreement massively overestimates label quality: unanimous agent labels stay wrong at rates that would be impossible for independent human annotators.

Cheap-proposer/expensive-verifier annotation cascades trace a predictable cost-quality frontier: verifying only flagged or disagreeing items achieves near full-expensive quality at a fraction of cost, and the frontier shape is estimable from a small pilot.

Iterative self-labeling loops (train on agent labels, relabel with the trained model, retrain) amplify the agent's initial systematic biases at a measurable per-round rate rather than washing them out, producing datasets that look cleaner and are more biased each round.

Agent annotation is guideline-brittle: paraphrasing the annotation guidelines shifts label distributions by as much as swapping the underlying model, making 'the guideline' an unreported experimental variable in agent-built datasets.

Annotation agents allowed to request extra evidence (zoomed crops, alternate frames) on self-flagged hard instances beat fixed-pipeline agents at matched cost, because evidence acquisition — not model quality — limits label accuracy on the hard tail.

Agent annotators erode dataset tails: rare classes are systematically relabeled toward frequent ones, so agent-curated datasets measurably shrink tail mass each generation, with compounding effects on models trained downstream.

Label provenance is recoverable: a classifier can distinguish models trained on agent-labeled versus human-labeled data using only behavioral probes, enabling post-hoc audits of dataset supply chains.

Cross-seed disagreement among annotation agents is a cheap detector of genuinely ambiguous instances: agent disagreement predicts human inter-annotator disagreement well enough to route only truly ambiguous items to humans.

Compiling natural-language annotation guidelines into executable checklists (ordered binary probes with evidence requirements) improves agent label consistency more than upgrading the base model, because guideline interpretation is the dominant noise source.

Given a fixed human budget inside an agent annotation loop, spending it on adjudicating agent disagreements dominates spending it on random spot-checks or gold seeding, and the advantage concentrates exactly where datasets matter most — the ambiguous tail.

LLM-guided where-to-look policies barely beat brute-force grid scanning at matched crop budgets: most of the reported benefit of visual-search agents comes from having more pixels, not from intelligent search.

Agent fixations track bottom-up saliency, not the question: look-location distributions barely shift across different questions about the same image, revealing that 'question-guided' viewing in current loops is mostly generic salience.
A single forced confirmatory zoom on the claimed evidence region after answering cuts hallucinated-detail errors at negligible cost, because most hallucinations are never re-inspected by the loop.

Loop step order is a first-class variable: agents that draft an answer before zooming anchor on the draft and ignore contradicting crop evidence, while zoom-first ordering avoids the anchor at identical compute.

Agents cannot judge evidence sufficiency — prompted 'can you answer now?' probes are near chance — but a small stopping head trained on loop traces predicts sufficiency well, converting wasted fixed-depth loops into adaptive ones.

Accuracy versus number of accumulated crops is non-monotone: beyond a small working set, added crops interfere with earlier evidence and net accuracy declines, giving each controller a measurable optimal working-set size.

Enumeration loops that mark counted instances repair the systematic undercount of one-shot VLM counting on dense scenes: the fix is loop structure, not model scale, and the crossover density is measurable.

In multi-view settings, language-reasoned next-view selection adds little over random next views except on the occlusion-limited subset — and that subset is identifiable in advance, telling systems when view planning is worth its cost.

Maintaining a persistent low-resolution global view alongside high-resolution foveal crops beats sequences of uniform crops at equal token budget, because zoom loops measurably lose global context — scale and off-crop relations — when the overview is dropped.
Multi-agent visual debate converges to the shared percept, not the truth: same-backbone debaters agree more and stay wrong on perception errors, with stated confidence rising while accuracy is flat.

Vision-agent ensemble gains come from vision-encoder diversity, not LLM diversity: mixing LLMs over a shared encoder yields little, while mixing encoders under one LLM captures most of the full-ensemble gain.

Role prompts change transcripts, not outcomes: skeptic/looker/reasoner roles only improve multi-agent vision accuracy when the roles receive different inputs, so engineered information asymmetry — not persona text — is the active ingredient.

At matched inference compute, majority voting matches debate and judge-arbitration on perception tasks: the deliberation transcript is compute repackaged, and reported protocol advantages vanish under iso-compute accounting.

An adversarial checker agent instructed to construct the disconfirming view — the specific crop or transformation that would falsify the claim — beats confirmation-style verification at equal cost, importing falsification-seeking into vision loops.

Hallucinated details become sticky in multi-agent transcripts: once an unsupported visual claim is repeated twice, its adoption probability by other agents exceeds its correction probability, quantifying error contagion as a system property.

Splitting dense scenes among parallel agents pays only above a measurable object-density threshold: below it, coordination and double-counting costs exceed parallel gains, and the crossover is predictable from single-agent working-set limits.

Tool-set diversity decorrelates agent errors where temperature and prompt diversity do not: assigning different tool access to ensemble members lowers error correlation and lifts ensemble accuracy beyond any sampling-based diversity at equal cost.

Manager-worker hierarchies only beat flat self-verification when workers use different tools or views: a manager reviewing same-tool worker outputs is redundant compute, and the condition can be tested by toggling worker heterogeneity.

In multi-agent vision exchanges, message confidence markers predict claim adoption more than attached image evidence does: agents weigh rhetoric over pixels, making persuasive-but-wrong agents systematically dangerous in mixed pipelines.

VLM-judge failures decompose into perception failures (cannot see the difference) and criterion failures (sees it, wrong rubric): an oracle-perception protocol — feeding ground-truth descriptions instead of pixels — cleanly splits the two and tells you whether to fix eyes or rubric.

The generator-verifier gap that powers self-improvement in code and math is absent for perception: judging a visual answer requires the same percept as producing it, so same-model visual judges provide no exploitable training signal.

Judges given executable rubrics — per-item binary checks each requiring pointed image evidence — agree with humans more than holistic judges at equal cost, converting judging from perception-plus-taste into a sequence of verifiable micro-perceptions.

Position and order biases in visual pairwise judging can be converted from a flaw into a filter: keeping only swap-consistent judgments yields a subset with much higher human agreement, giving a usable reliability lever without retraining.

Visual-judge self-preference is stylistic, not substantive: rewriting identical answer content in another model family's style moves judge preference, showing the bias lives in surface-form recognition rather than content assessment.

Ensembles of small diverse judges beat one frontier judge at matched cost only when their vision encoders differ: judge-ensemble value is a decorrelation phenomenon, predictable from pairwise judge error correlations before deployment.

Reference-based visual judging penalizes correct-but-different answers: judges overweight surface similarity to the reference, and the penalty on verified-equivalent paraphrases is large enough to flip system rankings that depend on judge scores.

VLM judges fail on dense geometric outputs but recover with rendered comparisons: overlaying prediction-vs-reference differences as visual diffs lifts judge accuracy on box and keypoint quality far above judging from raw pairs, mapping a capability boundary and its fix.

Using a VLM judge as a training reward has a measurable hacking onset: as optimization pressure grows, policies exploit judge blind spots at a predictable point, and the onset is a property of the judge-policy pair estimable before full training.

Pairwise visual-judgment intransitivity is a cheap reliability meter: cycle rate in a small tournament predicts judge-human agreement without any human labels, and cycle-repaired rankings recover accuracy the raw judge lacks.

End-to-end agent success is worse than the product of per-step success rates: shared context couples steps so that errors interact super-multiplicatively, and the negative interaction term grows with chain length.

Under mandatory iso-cost accounting — agent loop versus a bigger single model at matched dollars or FLOPs — a substantial share of reported loop gains disappears, exposing the field's default comparison (loop vs same-size single pass) as systematically flattering.

Agent loops should be selected on a measured latency-quality frontier: a 'marginal gain per marginal token' index computed from small pilots predicts which loop designs are Pareto-dominated before full evaluation, and typical configurations sit far inside the frontier.

A five-way failure taxonomy — mis-grounding, stale state, tool misuse, premature stop, over-looping — covers the large majority of vision-agent failures across task families, making targeted repairs tractable and transferable.

Naive retry-on-failure raises hallucination rates: retries conditioned on failure context 'try harder' into confabulation, so second attempts are measurably less grounded than first attempts on the same instances.

Accumulated tool logs degrade late-loop decisions at fixed information content: verbatim history hurts relative to faithful summaries, contradicting the more-context-is-safer default for agent memory.

Run-to-run variance of full vision-agent pipelines has a stable component structure — controller sampling, prompt formatting, tool nondeterminism — and fixing the top component alone yields most of the achievable reproducibility, telling practitioners which knob to freeze first.

Controller intelligence is not the bottleneck: a small fine-tuned controller retains most of a frontier-controller system's end-task accuracy inside a fixed vision-agent scaffold, shifting the cost story of deployed vision agents.

Vision tools degrade inside loops because agents feed them off-distribution inputs — extreme crops, odd aspect ratios, resampled regions; measuring the in-loop degradation factor and adding an input-standardization wrapper recovers most of it without touching tools or controller.

Independently validated loop enhancements do not stack: pairwise interactions among verification, zooming, and voting are mostly zero or negative, so system builders need interaction-aware selection rather than feature accumulation.

Log-depth versus metric-depth regression targets act as fixed per-pixel gradient preconditioners, so the log target should win exactly on scenes whose depth-range ratio exceeds a predictable threshold and be irrelevant on shallow-range scenes.

Explicit per-pixel gradient rescaling applied to metric-depth training should recover most of the inverse-depth target's advantage, turning target-space folklore into a portable optimizer-side recipe.

Angular losses for surface-normal regression have a curvature blow-up near large errors that produces heavy-tailed gradient spikes early in training, and switching the early phase to bounded vector losses removes the spikes and the late-training accuracy debt they cause.

Polar (magnitude, angle) parameterization of optical-flow targets is ill-conditioned at small motions because angle gradients diverge as magnitude goes to zero, predicting a specific small-motion accuracy deficit that Cartesian targets do not have.

Signed-distance-field regression redistributes boundary-concentrated gradients across the whole image plane, and its benefit over per-pixel mask classification is predictable from how concentrated the mask-loss gradient field is (thin, elongated classes benefit; blob classes do not).

The Gaussian sigma of keypoint heatmap targets is an implicit learning-rate schedule, so annealing sigma during training should dominate any fixed sigma, and two runs ending at the same sigma but with different trajectories should end at measurably different accuracy.

Classification-over-bins beats direct regression for dense continuous targets mainly because it bounds per-pixel gradient magnitude, so regression with matched per-pixel gradient clipping should erase most of the gap.

Bounded offset parameterizations in dense detection heads win over absolute-coordinate regression not for representational reasons but because they compress the target range into the optimizer's stable step-size band, so an LR sweep should rescue absolute coordinates.

Softmax versus per-class sigmoid output parameterization in semantic segmentation determines whether co-occurring classes exchange gradients competitively, predicting opposite confusion dynamics for class pairs that frequently share boundaries.

Supervising dense outputs in a frequency-decomposed basis lets one schedule which spatial frequencies are learned when, and this only changes outcomes under truncated training budgets, pinpointing spectral acquisition order as a budget-dependent bottleneck.

Dice loss is an implicit instance-size reweighting schedule whose strength grows as predictions sharpen, predicting that dice beats cross-entropy only when the target size distribution is heavy-tailed beyond a measurable threshold.

Structured surrogate losses like Lovász hinge help exactly when a model's errors are spatially clustered, because their pixel-gradient coupling coordinates updates within an error blob, predicting the gain from a pre-training error-autocorrelation measurement.

Focal loss is functionally an annealed hard-pixel selection schedule: replacing it with explicit top-k pixel selection whose k follows focal's shrinking effective-support trajectory should reproduce its gains, killing the reweighting-form story.

Cross-entropy training drives dense-head logit norms to grow roughly logarithmically, imposing a hidden effective-LR decay on decision geometry; norm-controlled heads should therefore need explicit schedule compensation, exposing an unacknowledged coupling between loss and schedule.

Boundary-region learning is gradient-starved until interiors saturate, making interior-then-boundary acquisition an optimization-forced order; boundary emphasis should therefore only matter under short training budgets, with a predictable crossover.

Class-frequency loss reweighting interacts destructively with momentum: rare-class gradient bursts get smeared into subsequent unrelated batches, so reweighting gains should shrink as momentum grows, an interaction nobody tunes for.

Whether combining two dense losses helps is determined by the spatial structure of their per-pixel gradient disagreement: structured disagreement (different losses own different pixel populations) yields complementary gains, diffuse disagreement yields averaging.

Temperature in pixel-level contrastive objectives sets the effective number of negatives that receive gradient, and the right temperature is determined by the intra-class visual diversity of the dataset, predicting opposite tuning directions for homogeneous versus diverse datasets.

Pairwise/structured consistency terms in dense losses act mostly as spatial gradient-noise dampers, so replacing them with content-blind local gradient smoothing should reproduce the bulk of their reported gains.

Asymmetric region losses (Tversky-style) change ranking quality only when class overlap in feature space is itself asymmetric; otherwise they merely slide along the precision-recall curve, which threshold-free ranking metrics will expose.

Adam's advantage over SGD for transformer-based dense predictors is concentrated in attention-projection layers with heavy-tailed gradient distributions, so adaptive preconditioning applied only to those layers should recover most of the gap at SGD-like memory cost.

Adam's beta2 is a rare-event memory horizon: rare-class gradient bursts decay out of the second-moment estimate between occurrences, so rare-class accuracy should depend on beta2 with a crossover predicted by the class recurrence interval.

Most of weight decay's accuracy effect in fine-tuned dense predictors is mediated by the final head's logit-scale dynamics, so decaying only the head should reproduce full-network decay, contradicting the feature-regularization story.

Global gradient clipping in dense training triggers almost exclusively on a tiny, stable population of image-crop configurations, so it functions as implicit example down-weighting; removing those crops should reproduce clipping's benefit without any clipping.
Weight EMA helps dense prediction in proportion to augmentation strength because it averages out augmentation-induced weight oscillations, predicting near-zero EMA gains in weak-augmentation regimes.

Layer-wise LR decay and shortened training are two projections of one variable, total feature rotation, so (decay factor, schedule length) pairs producing equal rotation should produce equal dense-task transfer, collapsing a 2D tuning grid to 1D.

Sign-based and update-normalized optimizers help dense training only when inter-layer gradient-scale disparity exceeds a threshold, because their active ingredient is per-layer update-norm equalization, which plain SGD plus per-layer normalization reproduces.

Gradient accumulation is not equivalent to large-batch training for dense models with batch normalization, because BN statistics see micro-batches; the folklore equivalence silently breaks and the break size is predictable from BN's batch-size noise curve.

The folklore that loss scale does not matter under Adam fails for dense per-pixel-mean losses whose magnitude approaches Adam's epsilon, predicting resolution-dependent silent undertraining and a one-line epsilon fix.

The linear batch-size/LR scaling rule breaks earlier for dense tasks than classification because pixels within an image are correlated samples, making the critical batch size a function of intra-image gradient correlation rather than image count.

Warmup in dense fine-tuning primarily protects the randomly initialized head-to-backbone interface, so warming up only the head's learning rate should reproduce full-network warmup and identify whose instability warmup actually fixes.

For dense prediction, the tail integral of the LR schedule is a sufficient statistic: cosine, step, and poly schedules matched on late-phase LR integral should produce equal accuracy, reducing schedule-shape debates to one number.

Final learning rate sets a spatial-frequency noise floor: boundary-band accuracy keeps improving as final LR decreases long after interior accuracy saturates, following a power law that tells practitioners when further decay is wasted.

The last-epochs augmentation-off trick works as a short distribution re-adaptation phase whose required length is set by augmentation strength and normalization-statistics inertia, not by total training length, predicting a fixed small step budget suffices at any scale.

Cyclic-LR snapshot ensembles for dense prediction gain almost entirely at spatial decision boundaries because cycles re-randomize low-curvature boundary placements while interiors are pinned, predicting ensemble gains concentrate in trimap bands.

Mean-validation-loss early stopping systematically truncates late-acquired classes in dense training because per-class acquisition is staggered, so class-resolved stopping criteria should recover rare-class accuracy that standard practice silently discards.

Warmup length requirements scale inversely with pixels-per-batch, not images-per-batch, because dense gradient noise is set by supervised-pixel count, predicting high-resolution training needs far less warmup than folklore prescribes.

The freeze-then-unfreeze fine-tuning ritual creates a measurable gradient shock at the unfreeze step, and gradual unfreezing only helps when that shock exceeds a threshold, giving a one-measurement rule for whether the gentler schedule is worth implementing.

Constant-LR-plus-EMA matches decayed schedules on interior-dominated metrics but systematically lags on boundary-sensitive metrics, because weight averaging only mimics decay where the local loss is quadratic, which boundary directions violate.

Strong-augmentation-early, weak-late ordering beats the reverse only under short budgets, because high-LR phases absorb high-variance augmentation gradients while low-LR phases cannot, predicting an ordering-by-budget interaction with a crossover.

The linear-probe-then-finetune advantage for dense tasks can be earned adaptively: hold the backbone until the head's gradient norm falls below a fixed fraction of the backbone's, then release, matching tuned two-stage recipes without tuning the stage boundary.

Dense fine-tuning proceeds in two intrinsic phases, normalization/bias adaptation first and weight-matrix rotation second, and the first phase alone accounts for most in-domain gain, making the phase boundary a natural budget knob.

Forgetting of pretraining abilities during dense fine-tuning is episodic rather than gradual, concentrated in identifiable step windows tied to LR milestones and batch composition, so cheap interventions targeted at those windows should preserve abilities at negligible cost.

Head initialization scale bifurcates dense fine-tuning into feature-reuse and feature-rewrite regimes at a sharp threshold, making one init hyperparameter a regime selector that explains bimodal fine-tuning outcomes.

The weight-update matrices of full dense-task fine-tuning have systematically higher effective rank than classification fine-tuning on matched backbones, quantifying why low-rank adaptation recipes ported from classification underfit dense tasks.

Dense fine-tuning exits the linearly-connected basin of its initialization within a few hundred steps while classification fine-tuning stays connected for most of training, giving a sharp geometric signature of how much dense adaptation restructures solutions.

Intermediate-task fine-tuning helps dense targets mostly by delivering a well-conditioned head and normalization state rather than better features, so transplanting only those components from the intermediate model should reproduce most of the stepping-stone gain.
The depth of the early-fine-tuning accuracy dip carries no information about final dense-task quality, debunking the practice of culling fine-tuning runs by their first-epochs behavior.

The folklore 10x head-LR multiplier is a proxy for equalizing head and backbone adaptation timescales, so the optimal multiplier should collapse toward 1 as head initialization quality improves, unifying two separate fine-tuning rituals.

Re-initializing the final backbone block before dense fine-tuning helps precisely when the pretraining objective's terminal computations conflict with dense decoding, a conflict measurable as high initial gradient opposition in that block.

Frequency-resolved error curves of dense predictors collapse onto one universal acquisition trajectory when time is reparameterized by integrated learning rate, making spectral acquisition order a schedule-invariant law rather than an architecture story.

Dense models acquire texture-based discrimination before shape integration within a single training run, and stronger appearance augmentation delays the crossover rather than removing it, making cue reliance a scheduled phase rather than a fixed property.

Within-class appearance variance, not class frequency, is the dominant determinant of when a class is acquired during segmentation training, inverting the standard imbalance-centric account of late learners.

Delayed generalization (grokking-like) exists in dense prediction: under strong weight decay and small data, validation boundary quality jumps long after training loss saturates, with the delay controlled by the decay strength.

Early training at low resolution creates a persistent thin-structure deficit that equal-compute high-resolution fine-tuning cannot repair, establishing a within-run critical period for spatial detail.

Detection training acquires localization before classification in a fixed order (matched-box quality saturates while class accuracy still climbs), and the lag between the two phases predicts which errors dominate the final model.

Attention-map organization in ViT-based dense models undergoes an abrupt within-run transition (entropy drop plus locality emergence), and dense-task transferability of the features begins rising only after this transition, making it a measurable readiness marker.

Class acquisition order in dense training is optimization-forced, not data-forced: aggressive class-balanced resampling shifts acquisition times but preserves the order, exposing a fixed difficulty hierarchy that data curricula cannot reorder.

Epoch-wise double descent in dense prediction is spatially localized: boundary-band validation error is non-monotone over training while interior error descends monotonically, so the phenomenon's visibility depends on which metric a paper reports.

Within-run neural collapse in segmentation heads is class-asymmetric: frequent-class features collapse toward their class means early while rare-class features never fully collapse, and the residual within-class variance identifies which classes still benefit from continued training.

Interior and boundary pixels of the same instance send systematically conflicting gradients through shared decoder features, and the depth at which the conflict peaks tells you where decoupled decoding pays off.

In joint segmentation+depth training, destructive gradient conflict is confined to the top decoder layers, so splitting only those layers should recover nearly all of the fully-split architecture's benefit, replacing task-architecture folklore with a conflict-localization rule.

Deep-supervision auxiliary heads work as per-depth gradient-norm equalizers, so removing them and directly rescaling per-block learning rates to match their induced gradient profile should reproduce their accuracy, collapsing an architectural ritual into an optimizer setting.
Optimal task weights in multi-task dense training are those that equalize per-task gradient noise-to-signal ratios measured mid-run, replacing grid search over weights with a two-measurement rule.

Cross-view consistency gradients in augmentation-consistency training act as beneficial exploration noise early and harmful drag late, predicting that the standard constant or ramp-up consistency weight is backwards at the end of training.

Confusable class pairs in segmentation exhibit zero-sum oscillation during training, with epoch-to-epoch accuracy fluctuations that are anti-correlated pairwise, revealing that late training redistributes a fixed decision boundary rather than improving both classes.

The classification and box-regression branches of dense detectors conflict on shared features with a characteristic time signature (regression gradients shrink as boxes converge while classification persists), explaining mechanistically why decoupled-head designs win and when they stop mattering.

In panoptic training, stuff-region gradients numerically dominate thing-region gradients through sheer pixel count, suppressing instance-discrimination learning; branch-specific batch composition (alternating thing-rich and stuff-rich crops) should fix this without any loss reweighting.

Teacher-student dense self-distillation has a two-phase structure with a measurable phase boundary: before teacher-student agreement crosses a threshold the teacher acts as a denoiser, after it the loop locks in student errors, so distillation weight should be scheduled against measured agreement, not time.

Cut-and-paste mixing augmentations shift a large share of the boundary-gradient budget onto artificial paste boundaries, so their net effect flips sign between interior-dominated and boundary-sensitive evaluation, resolving contradictory reports about their value for segmentation.

Frozen-BN folklore in detection fine-tuning works because small-batch BN statistic noise acts as an uncontrolled multiplicative perturbation on all downstream computation, so noise-corrected BN (larger virtual batches) should erase the freezing advantage and flip the recommendation at scale.

BN running-statistics momentum is an implicit schedule that should be tied to the LR schedule: as LR decays, statistics lag the (now slowly moving) weights less, so the fixed default momentum over-smooths late training and under-smooths early training, and matching the two schedules removes a persistent train-eval gap.

The BN-vs-GN choice for dense training is governed by a two-dimensional phase boundary in (images per batch, pixels per image): BN wins only above a critical image count that itself grows with resolution, giving a chartable decision diagram instead of contradictory folklore.

fp16 training with loss scaling loses rare-class gradient contributions first, because their sparse, small-magnitude gradients sit closest to the underflow boundary, creating a class-selective precision tax that fp32 and bf16 do not share.

Multi-resolution dense training works smoothly for LayerNorm architectures but silently degrades BN-based hybrids, because BN statistics are resolution-dependent while LN normalizes per token, predicting a normalization-conditioned verdict on variable-resolution schedules.

BN's train-mode stochasticity is a load-bearing regularizer in dense training: reproducing its measured noise distribution via explicit activation-noise injection under fixed statistics should recover most of BN's generalization advantage over deterministic normalization.

In normalization-free dense training, adaptive gradient clipping thresholds map onto an equivalent BN batch-size curve, unifying two stability mechanisms as one effective constraint on relative update size and predicting threshold transfer across tasks without tuning.

bf16 and fp16 dense training differ mainly through loss-scaling dynamics rather than representational precision: fp16 with an oracle (perfect, non-adaptive) loss scale should match bf16, isolating the real cost of fp16 as scale-controller misbehavior during gradient-magnitude transients.

Online hard-example mining is a feedback dynamical system with two regimes: a stable regime where the mined set evolves slowly and mining helps, and a limit-cycle regime where the mined set flips between populations and mining underperforms plain training, with the regime identifiable online from mined-set overlap.

The crop-size folklore for segmentation decomposes into a normalization-statistics component and a context component, and controlled statistic-swapping shows which one carries the large-crop advantage, with opposite architectural implications.

Per-pixel loss computation is massively redundant: the safe pixel-subsampling rate for loss evaluation is set by the spatial correlation length of the gradient field, giving a measurable dial that trades compute for nothing until a sharp knee.

At fixed pixels-per-batch, spending the budget on more images with smaller crops beats fewer images with larger crops for gradient-noise reasons, except where context genuinely binds, giving a decomposable rule for the most common memory tradeoff in dense training.

Within-epoch presentation order leaves a measurable recency imprint on dense models at high learning rates: images seen late in the final epoch are predicted better than statistically identical images seen early, quantifying an ordering bias no one controls for.

Gradients from overlapping random crops of the same image are correlated almost linearly in their overlap area, so standard crop samplers waste batch slots; overlap-aware crop sampling recovers the wasted effective batch size for free.

Dense contrastive pretraining with within-image negatives learns positional shortcuts (discriminating by location rather than content), a failure mode absent with cross-image negatives, detectable by a position-decoding probe and fixable by position-debiased sampling.

The gradient noise scale of dense training drifts by an order of magnitude within a single run (unlike classification's comparative stability), so any fixed batch size is wrong for most of the run and a noise-tracking batch-size ramp captures measurable gains.

Photometric augmentation strength and learning rate are partially interchangeable noise sources in dense training, with iso-accuracy contours revealing a measurable exchange rate, so recipes tuned at one LR silently mis-tune augmentation at another.

Channel dropout and spatially structured dropout in dense decoders trade places as decoder width changes, because their effective noise targets (feature redundancy vs spatial redundancy) scale oppositely with width, predicting a width-conditioned reversal that folklore misses.

Stochastic depth in ViT dense fine-tuning is an implicit layer-wise LR decay in disguise (deeper blocks receive fewer effective updates), so its tuned drop-rate profile should be reproducible by an explicit LLRD profile matched to expected update rates, unifying two rituals.

Label smoothing in segmentation trades boundary representation quality for interior stability: it collapses the logit structure that encodes soft class transitions at boundaries, predicting opposite effects on interior and boundary metrics that aggregate mIoU conceals.

The ramp-up period folklore for auxiliary regularizer weights exists to protect training until the supervised gradient stabilizes, so an adaptive ramp triggered by measured gradient-norm stabilization should match hand-tuned ramps across setups with zero tuning.

Wide random-resize ranges pay their cost only early: scale-range annealing (wide early, narrow late) should match full wide-range training on scale robustness while recovering the late-phase accuracy that wide ranges tax, resolving the scale-augmentation dilemma as a scheduling problem.

Weight decay and strong augmentation regularize an overlapping subspace in dense training (both suppress feature-norm growth on nuisance directions), predicting substitutability with a measurable exchange rate and explaining why heavily augmented recipes tolerate near-zero decay.

Geometric augmentations (flips, rotations) and photometric augmentations act on dense training through different optimization channels, geometric ones reshaping the per-pixel loss landscape correlation structure and photometric ones adding gradient noise, predicting non-interchangeable, task-dependent roles that strength-matching experiments will separate.

Loss spikes in dense training are triggered by reproducible image-crop-augmentation conjunctions, not random batch bad luck: the same content configurations spike across seeds, making spike-trigger mining a dataset diagnostic rather than a stability mystery.

Backbone parameters in dense training sit at the edge of stability (top curvature hovering near the 2/LR boundary) like classification networks do, but dense decoder heads systematically do not, revealing a two-regime landscape that schedule design currently ignores.

Divergence events in ViT dense fine-tuning are preceded by attention-entropy collapse in a small identifiable set of heads, providing an early-warning signal several hundred steps ahead of the loss explosion and a targeted intervention (per-head temperature) that prevents it.

Dense fine-tuning divergence obeys a universal boundary in the head-to-backbone update-ratio: across tasks and architectures, runs diverge when the sustained ratio exceeds a shared threshold, yielding a one-number stability criterion and a ratio-capping guard that replaces conservative global LR reduction.

Recovery from training spikes is spatially unequal: interior and frequent-class accuracy heals within hundreds of steps while rare-class and boundary accuracy exhibits hysteresis lasting many epochs, so a run's spike history taxes exactly the metrics that aggregate curves hide.

Tail-averaging (SWA-style) of dense-training checkpoints improves interiors but degrades or fails to improve boundary placement when averaged checkpoints still disagree structurally at boundaries, making the disagreement decomposition, not flat-minima intuition, the correct adoption criterion.
